lesson.title: The Forwarding Table: A Router's Cheat Sheet for Every Packet
lesson.summary: A forwarding table is the lean, fast lookup structure a router's hardware checks for every arriving packet to decide which outgoing interface to send it out, distinct from the richer table used to compute those decisions.
lesson.body:
Forwarding, as you have seen, has to happen for every single packet a router touches, often thousands or millions of times per second on a busy link. That kind of speed rules out anything fancy: a router cannot re-derive the best path to a destination from scratch each time a packet shows up. Instead it consults a forwarding table, a compact structure built ahead of time that maps a destination address, or more precisely a range of destination addresses, directly to an outgoing interface and, on a local link, the next hop's hardware address.

Because forwarding tables are read constantly and updated relatively rarely, real routers implement them in specialized hardware built for one job: extremely fast lookups. A typical entry does not list a single destination address but a whole prefix, a block of addresses that share the same leading bits, so one entry can cover an entire network rather than every individual host on it. When a packet arrives, the router performs what is called a longest prefix match: among all the entries whose prefix contains the packet's destination address, it picks the most specific one, the one with the longest matching prefix, since that entry describes the closest, most accurate route.

For example, a forwarding table might contain an entry for the prefix 10.1.0.0/16 pointing out interface eth0, and a more specific entry for 10.1.5.0/24 pointing out eth1. A packet addressed to 10.1.5.20 matches both entries, but the router uses the /24 entry because it is more specific, and sends the packet out eth1. A packet addressed to 10.1.9.3 matches only the /16 entry and goes out eth0. It is worth remembering that the forwarding table itself does not decide what the best path is, it is simply the fast, ready to use answer sheet that gets filled in by the routing process, the subject of the next few chapters.
